title: Define proof-doctor verdict schema and blocker taxonomy
description:
## What
Define the typed verdict schema for proof-doctor output. Include proof phase, command intent, RCH binary/version/config source, worker selection, sync result, whether Cargo/rustc was reached, source/test verdict, local-fallback detection, dirty-tree ownership, Bead ownership, and next action.

## Why
FrankenTerm proof lanes repeatedly fail in ways that look similar in logs but mean very different things. A pre-Cargo RCH wrapper failure, a real rustc compile error, an active dirty-tree conflict, and an inconclusive timeout must never collapse into the same status.

## How
Design enums and JSON/TOON envelopes first. Keep the schema stable enough for robot-mode callers and proof ledger ingestion. Use explicit reason codes rather than prose-only status.

## Risks
Overly broad taxonomy can become unmaintained. Keep the first version focused on observed proof blockers and leave extension points for later.

## Acceptance
- Schema distinguishes infrastructure, source, test, ownership, dirty-tree, fallback, and inconclusive states.
- Every verdict has an operator-facing message plus machine reason code.
- The design references existing proof-ledger and release-report surfaces without duplicating them.

title: Add proof-doctor command and robot-mode surface
description:
## What
Expose proof doctor through a human CLI command and a robot-mode surface. The command should accept the intended proof command, optional Bead id, optional expected package/test filter, and output format json/toon.

## Why
Agents and humans both need the same truth surface. A CLI-only tool helps operators, while robot-mode output lets other agents decide whether to run, defer, comment, or message the owner.

## How
Route through existing command patterns in crates/frankenterm and typed structures in frankenterm-core. Prefer a dry-run/preflight command first; do not execute arbitrary proof commands inside the first implementation unless policy and audit handling are explicit.

## Risks
A command that shells out unsafely would become a policy problem. The first pass should parse and describe proof intent rather than becoming a new execution engine.

## Acceptance
- Human CLI output is concise and explains the top blocker.
- Robot output is stable JSON/TOON with the full verdict schema.
- The command refuses local Cargo proof recommendations when repo policy requires RCH.

title: Implement proof-doctor preflight for RCH and dirty workspace state
description:
## What
Implement a proof-doctor preflight that runs before expensive proof lanes. It should inspect effective RCH config sources, binary path/version, whether external timeout controls are honored, current git dirty paths, Beads assignees for active work, file reservations where available, and whether requested proof paths overlap active dirty files.

## Why
Today agents discover these blockers only after a long RCH sync or compile. Preflight should warn before a doomed run and should name the owner or Bead when the blocker is not local to the current task.

## How
Use structured local probes only: git status/diff metadata, br JSON, optional Agent Mail reservation data, and RCH config/status JSON. Do not invoke local Cargo as preflight. Keep expensive proof commands separate.

## Risks
Preflight can become stale if it races with another agent. Verdicts must include timestamps and clearly say they are advisory until the proof command starts.

## Acceptance
- Preflight flags old RCH binaries/config-source mismatches before remote execution.
- Preflight identifies dirty paths and active Beads that likely own them.
- Preflight exits successfully with a machine-readable WARN/BLOCK verdict rather than throwing opaque shell errors.

title: [idea-wizard][redactor] Make streaming overflow progress Unicode-safe and evidence-honest
description:
## Background

The current recovery package includes a redactor multibyte overflow fix candidate. The underlying risk is that degenerate streaming caps can fail to make progress when pending data begins with a multibyte UTF-8 scalar. The same area also has an evidence semantics question around lossy byte accounting.

## Goal

Guarantee streaming overflow drains make progress for multibyte UTF-8 prefixes, preserve bounded-memory behavior, and design honest redaction evidence semantics for original bytes and bytes replaced.

## Non-goals

Do not weaken redaction coverage, remove privacy protections, or land schema wording that overclaims proof. Do not use local Cargo as final proof.

## Acceptance

The family lands a Unicode-safe cap floor and regression, designs the evidence schema correction, updates integration points, and captures RCH-retained proof plus any privacy attestation update once RCH and disk pressure recover.

title: move FTS5 indexing off the capture-write transaction
description:
# Background

Follow-up to ft-kcsae (answered). Live capture path in storage.rs
writes synchronously INTO the FTS5 index via three AFTER-triggers:

    storage.rs:169  output_segments_ai AFTER INSERT  → INSERT INTO output_segments_fts
    storage.rs:173  output_segments_ad AFTER DELETE  → fts delete
    storage.rs:177  output_segments_au AFTER UPDATE  → fts delete + insert

Every captured segment pays the inverted-index rebuild cost before
`append_segment_sync` returns (storage.rs:12308 → 12335 INSERT INTO
output_segments). Under 200-pane fanout the trigger cost is paid 200x
per-wire-tick.

# Existing primitives that can be reused

- `fts_pane_progress` table (storage.rs:472) — already tracks per-pane
  last-indexed-seq with resumable offsets.
- `sync_fts_on_startup(conn, FtsSyncConfig)` (storage.rs:16131) — the
  batched catchup engine. Currently only fires at startup.
- `FtsSyncConfig` (storage.rs:2363) — batch_size=100, max_batch_bytes=1
  MB, commit_progress per batch. Ready knobs.

# Proposal

1. Drop the three AFTER triggers on output_segments.
2. Add a writer-thread ticker (every N seconds OR after M segments
   since last catchup) that runs `sync_fts_on_startup` with the
   existing FtsSyncConfig and uses `fts_pane_progress` to pick up
   where it left off.
3. Gate behind a `storage.fts_indexing_mode = 'sync' | 'deferred'`
   config flag; default 'sync' at first, flip to 'deferred' after a
   round of search-freshness observability.
4. Expose catchup-lag (now - max(fts_pane_progress.last_indexed_at))
   as a metric so operators can spot index drift.

# Risk

- Search freshness becomes eventual (default lag = catchup interval).
- FTS rows can briefly diverge from output_segments during a crash
  between INSERT and the next catchup tick — acceptable because
  `sync_fts_on_startup` already handles gap recovery on startup.

# Measurement prerequisite

Before landing: add a bench that measures `append_segment_sync` p99
under a 200-pane load with FTS5 enabled (current) vs. triggers
disabled + deferred catchup. If the gap is not material, don't ship —
the synchronous path is simpler and the trigger tax might be in the
noise given SQLite's WAL + page cache.
close_reason: Opt-in deferred FTS indexing landed as d74401c6. Added StorageConfig.defer_fts_triggers: bool (default false, preserves current sync behavior). When true, StorageHandle::with_config executes DROP TRIGGER IF EXISTS on output_segments_a[iud] immediately after initialize_schema, so new segment writes no longer synchronously rebuild FTS inverted-index pages. Callers are responsible for periodic sync_fts() invocation; the fts_pane_progress + sync_fts_on_startup engine already handles resumable batched catchup. Verified via 4 new regression tests in fts_sync_tests (17 total passing): fts_sync_mode_indexes_on_insert (baseline), fts_deferred_mode_does_not_index_on_insert (post-DROP empty FTS), fts_deferred_mode_catchup_indexes_all_segments (500 segments → catchup → 500 indexed, second catchup is no-op), fts_deferred_mode_catchup_resumes_across_rounds (5 rounds × 100 segments interleaved with catchup, each round indexes exactly 100). Surfaced but did NOT fix: pre-existing seq=0 off-by-one in sync_fts_for_pane (WHERE seq > last_indexed_seq excludes fresh pane's seq=0 segment) — tests use seq 1..=N, separate bead for that fix.

title: latency QoE guardrail accepts non-finite samples and percentiles
description:
Phase 3 audit finding in latency_stages::slo_validation.

Evidence:
- crates/frankenterm-core/src/latency_stages/slo_validation.rs:36-67 exposes QoESLO.percentile/target and QoEMeasurement.value as public serde f64 values, with no validation method on QoEGuardrailConfig.
- crates/frankenterm-core/src/latency_stages/slo_validation.rs:180-198 constructs the guardrail and records measurements directly, including NaN or infinity.
- crates/frankenterm-core/src/latency_stages/slo_validation.rs:217-220 sorts with partial_cmp(...).unwrap_or(Equal) and computes an index from percentile * len without checking that percentile is finite and in range.
- crates/frankenterm-core/src/latency_stages/slo_validation.rs:372-380 repeats the same pattern for current_percentile().

Why it matters: malformed telemetry can produce unstable percentile selection or return non-finite values through health/reporting paths.

Proposed remediation: reject or ignore non-finite measurement values, require finite percentiles in 0.0..=1.0, and use total_cmp after sanitization. Add unit/proptest coverage for NaN, +/-Inf, negative percentiles, and >1 percentiles.

- crates/frankenterm-core/src/capacity_governor.rs:59-79 accepts raw f64 PressureSignals for cpu_utilization, memory_utilization, load_average_1m, and io_pressure.
- crates/frankenterm-core/src/capacity_governor.rs:105-113 derives health_tier from f64::max over cpu/memory/io and forwards the result to HealthTier::from_ratio.
- crates/frankenterm-core/src/runtime_telemetry.rs:160-169 maps ratios with ordered < comparisons; NaN falls through to Black there, but capacity_governor compute_decision uses separate >= comparisons.
- crates/frankenterm-core/src/capacity_governor.rs:522-524,534-535,582-584 compares raw signal values with >=. If a collector returns NaN for CPU, memory, or load average, the corresponding overload guard is false.
- crates/frankenterm-core/src/capacity_governor.rs:862-873 tests health_tier only with finite CPU/memory values.

Impact:
A telemetry ingestion glitch can make one pressure dimension disappear from the enforcement path while audit health may show a different tier. That is a fail-open sensor-domain bug in a backpressure controller.

Proposed remediation:
Normalize or validate PressureSignals before evaluation. Reject/convert non-finite CPU, memory, and io ratios to a fail-closed high-pressure value; reject/convert non-finite load_average_1m similarly. Add tests proving arbitrary NaN/inf pressure inputs cannot produce Allow for heavy work when the corrupted field is the decisive pressure dimension.
close_reason: Landed in 3e73e9eb9: capacity_governor normalizes non-finite pressure signals before evaluation, maps NaN CPU/memory/io ratios to fail-closed high pressure, maps NaN load_average_1m to the heavy-work block threshold, and adds NaN pressure proptest coverage. Verified: env FT_LOCAL_NOFORK=1 FT_LOCAL_TARGET=/tmp/ft-cod7-wm40o-proof-target scripts/cargo-local.sh check -p frankenterm-core --lib --no-default-features passed; targeted cargo-local test for nan_pressure_inputs_do_not_allow_heavy_work passed. title: [mock-code-finder][gui-lua] Wire GUI startup/attach hooks and debug overlay log stream

title: [deadlock-audit] spsc_ring_buffer.rs:157: SPSC send_with_cx misses mid-flight cancel while waiting for not_full
description:
Audit: /deadlock-finder-and-fixer concurrency scan of crates/frankenterm-core/src.

Real hazard: SpscProducer::send_with_cx checks cx.checkpoint() before waiting, then awaits a plain asupersync Notify at spsc_ring_buffer.rs:157. The function docs promise that cancellation during a blocked notified.await returns Err(value), but no select-race or cx-aware wait is used. If the queue is full and no consumer frees capacity after the caller cancels, the sender remains suspended until a not_full notification or close. This matches the known asupersync mid-flight-cancel gap for waits that are only checkpointed before suspension.

Expected fix direction: race notified.await against a cx-cancel watcher or introduce a shared cx-aware notify helper; add a LabRuntime regression where the queue is full, send_with_cx is blocked, cx is cancelled, and no receiver drains.
close_reason: Fixed spsc send_with_cx mid-flight cancel via select-raced notify wait; rch spsc_ring_buffer tests passed.

title: [golden-artifacts] error renderer: 1 golden for 17+ Error variants, existing one failing on Wezterm/wezterm casing drift
description:
## The gap

`crates/frankenterm-core/src/output/error_renderer.rs` is the
single source of human-readable + JSON error rendering for ft.
`Error` (in `src/error.rs:151`) is a 17+ variant enum, each with a
distinct JSON shape (category, title, recovery_steps, hint).

Current golden coverage: **exactly one** test, `typed_pane_not_found_renderer_matches_golden` (line 929).

Worse: that one golden is currently FAILING. The repo has both:
- `tests/fixtures/error_renderer_typed_pane_not_found.json` (frozen golden)
- `tests/fixtures/error_renderer_typed_pane_not_found.actual.json` (untracked, sitting there)

`diff` between them:

```
< "category": "Wezterm",
> "category": "wezterm",
```

The renderer started emitting lowercase `"wezterm"` and the `.actual`
has been left in the working tree as untracked output from a recent
failed test run. This is a real drift bug AND the test is silent in
CI because the .actual file isn't being noticed.

## Why this catches real defects (skill criterion)

The error-renderer JSON shape is a downstream contract: TypeScript
clients, MCP agents, the `ft doctor --json` consumers, and any
operator script that greps `error_code` rely on stable field names,
casing, and recovery_steps array shape. Today a developer can:

- Rename a field on an `Error` variant — landed green.
- Change category casing (the live drift bug) — landed green.
- Reorder recovery_steps — landed green.
- Add a new variant without a golden — landed green forever.

A 17-variant corpus with one golden per variant catches all four.

## Suggested implementation

1. **Audit the existing golden** — fix the `Wezterm`/`wezterm` drift,
   commit the corrected golden, delete the stale `.actual`.
2. **Add `.gitignore` entry** under `tests/fixtures/` to ignore
   `*.actual.json` so future failures don't leak as untracked clutter.
3. **Build a per-variant corpus** at
   `tests/fixtures/error_renderer/<variant>.json` with one golden per
   `Error` enum variant: `Wezterm`, `Storage`, `Pattern`, `Workflow`,
   `Config`, `Policy`, `Io`, `Json`, `RuntimeOperation`, `PaneOperation`,
   `WatchdogWarningRead`, `Runtime`, `SetupError`, `Cancelled`,
   `Panicked` — at minimum.
4. **Test driver** `tests/conformance_error_renderer_corpus.rs` that
   constructs each variant with realistic inputs, runs through
   `ErrorRenderer::new(OutputFormat::Json).render(&err)`, and uses
   the existing `assert_matches_golden` (or insta) to diff against
   the corpus. UPDATE_GOLDENS workflow documented in the test
   header.
5. **Coverage assertion**: a meta-test enumerates `Error` variant
   names (via a manually-maintained list) and asserts that every
   one has a golden in the corpus dir. New `Error` variants without
   a golden fail this test.

## Out of scope

- Restructuring `Error` itself (`Runtime(String)` typed variants
  are tracked elsewhere).
- Plain-text formatter goldens (separate bead if needed).

## Acceptance criteria

- `tests/fixtures/error_renderer/<variant>.json` exists for every
  `Error` enum variant.
- `tests/conformance_error_renderer_corpus.rs` discovers and
  validates each.
- The Wezterm/wezterm casing drift is resolved (one direction or
  the other) and the test is green at HEAD.
- `tests/fixtures/.gitignore` excludes `*.actual.json`.
- The coverage meta-test fires red when a new `Error` variant is
  added without a golden.

## References

- `crates/frankenterm-core/src/output/error_renderer.rs:929`
  (existing single golden)
- `crates/frankenterm-core/src/error.rs:151` (the 17+ variant enum)
- `tests/fixtures/error_renderer_typed_pane_not_found.actual.json`
  (the .actual that's been sitting untracked)

Filed by cc_1 golden-artifacts audit, 2026-04-28.
close_reason: 15 per-variant goldens + coverage meta-test landed in b9eee48fd (bundled with cc_1's profiling beads commit due to a swarm index collision; the commit's diff includes all the corpus files + the Wezterm→wezterm drift fix + tests/fixtures/.gitignore). 16 tests pass under cargo test -p frankenterm-core --test conformance_error_renderer_corpus. Variants covered: wezterm, storage, pattern, workflow, config, policy, io, json, runtime_operation, pane_operation, watchdog_warning_read, runtime, setup_error, cancelled, panicked. Coverage meta-test fails red on a new Error variant landing without a golden OR an orphan golden remaining after a variant is deleted. Original drift bug (Wezterm vs ErrorCategory's #[serde(rename_all=snake_case)] resulting in 'wezterm') resolved by updating the frozen golden to match the renderer's actual output. The .actual.json drift artifact deleted; future ones gitignored.

title: mcp_missions::mcp_save_mission_tx_contract_to_path: non-atomic write corrupts tx contract on mid-write crash
description: crates/frankenterm-core/src/mcp_missions.rs:289-308 mcp_save_mission_tx_contract_to_path serializes a MissionTxContract and calls std::fs::write(path, json) directly. fs::write is NOT atomic — it open+truncate+write in a single sequence. If the process crashes (panic, SIGKILL, power loss, disk full mid-write) between truncate and final write, the target file is left truncated or with partial JSON. On next startup mcp_load_mission_tx_contract_from_path reads the partial file, serde_json::from_str bails with 'Invalid tx contract JSON', and the ENTIRE tx contract is lost — not the last update, the whole in-flight contract. Same shape applies to mcp_save_mission_contract_to_path if it exists via a copy-paste. The codebase already has the atomic-rename pattern for durable writes (config_profiles.rs:129-135 manifest writes, recorder_storage.rs:1061, rulesets.rs:182, wal_engine.rs:892). Fix: write to path.with_extension('json.tmp') first, then std::fs::rename to the final path. rename is atomic on POSIX and NTFS — the tx file is either the old contents or the new contents, never a truncated halfway state.
close_reason: Landed in 149f35d8 (fix(mcp_missions): atomic tmp+rename for mission/tx-contract saves). Both mcp_save_mission_tx_contract_to_path and mcp_save_mission_to_path now write to <path>.json.tmp and std::fs::rename onto the target. Two regression tests (save_tx_contract_is_atomic_rename_ft_wxqbt, save_mission_is_atomic_rename_ft_wxqbt) assert target file presence + .tmp-sibling absence + round-trip parseability. Verification of the tests blocked by pre-existing frankenterm-core compile blockers (ft-kqidb/uigpj/s2u51/zv3u9).

title: [OBS/BUILD] unicode_names.rs is 5.8MB / 140K lines — largest single file in the workspace (generated from Unicode 16.0 UCD)
description:
PHASE 3 PROJECT-WIDE ANALYSIS — Lens 5 (MAINTAINABILITY / BUILD-PERF) observation in GUI crate.

Site: crates/frankenterm-gui/src/unicode_names.rs

File stats:
- Size: 5.8MB
- Lines: 140,378
- Generated: 'ucd-generate names .' from Unicode 16.0.0 UCD per the 'DO NOT EDIT THIS FILE' header.
- Content: const lookup table NAMES: &'static [(&'static str, u32)] (Unicode character name → codepoint).

Structural observations:
- Largest single file in the workspace by ~6x. (Largest non-vendored core file is latency_stages.rs at 976KB; tracked in ft-l8s7v.)
- Generated, so file-level decomposition via sibling-module pattern is not the right answer (regeneration would clobber it).
- rustc must parse + typecheck this 140K-line file on every full rebuild; incremental builds amortize but cold builds take the hit.
- Repo-size impact: clones / mirrors carry the 5.8MB.

Possible remediations:
A) Move the table to a separate const-only sub-crate (frankenterm-gui-unicode-names) so changes to the GUI proper don't trigger this file's recompile.
B) Encode the table as a binary asset + lazy-load at startup via a tiny phf or fst + include_bytes! — runtime memory same, compile-time + repo-size both better.
C) Accept current trade-off — generated tables are well-trodden in Rust ecosystem (e.g., unicode-segmentation, idna), and 5.8MB / 140K lines is large but not unprecedented.

Why P4 (observation, not action item):
- The maintainer chose a generated-table approach deliberately (it's the standard pattern).
- No concrete operator-blocking incident.
- Compile-time + repo-size impact is real but likely already considered.

Acceptance: surface the trade-off so future cold-build perf or repo-size incidents have this on the candidate-list. No action required today.

title: mcp_proxy.rs: 3 RemoteProxyToolHandler::call runtime soft-block paths bypass observability counters
description:
## Sites
\`crates/frankenterm-core/src/mcp_proxy.rs:581-683\` — \`RemoteProxyToolHandler::call\` has FOUR distinct failure paths that all log via tracing but bump NO cumulative counter. The bus-level mount-failure counter (ft-8na0z+ft-59hlx) covers compose-time soft-skips; the destructive-tool-filter counter (ft-153dy) covers tool-level safety filtering. Neither covers RUNTIME per-call dispatch failures.

### Path C — Cx pre-flight checkpoint failed (L610-626)
The recently-shipped option-A++ for ft-xhj38 short-circuits BEFORE the per-server Mutex if `ctx.cx().checkpoint()` fails. Returns an Err with tracing::warn but no counter. Operators cannot answer "how often did proxy calls get pre-rejected because the caller cancelled?".

### Path D — Mutex poisoned (L628-633)
\`self.client.lock()\` returns Err if any prior thread that held the lock panicked. Returns an Err — but ALSO has NO tracing::warn, just the raw error message in the response. Worst observability of the four paths: silent both in counters AND logs.

### Path E — call_tool Err from remote (L666-682)
Remote MCP server rejected or transport failed. tracing::warn fires but no counter. This is the "remote actually rejected my destructive operation" path — operationally important.

### Path F — content decode failure (L641-654)
Remote returned content the local framework cannot map back. tracing::warn but no counter.

## Defect framing
Each of these is a runtime per-call soft-block on a destructive (mutating) operation. The local server has accepted the tool registration and dispatched the call; somewhere between Cx-checkpoint and remote response, the operation was silently rejected. Operators reading bus-level counters see "tool was registered, audit row was emitted" but cannot quantify "how many destructive operations actually got through to the remote vs got soft-blocked at the proxy boundary".

## Fix shape

### Single-counter shape (recommended)
Add `MCP_PROXY_CALL_DISPATCH_FAILURES: AtomicU64` plus public accessor and reset helper. Bump at all 4 paths. Doc-comment enumerates the 4 contributing sources (matches the multi-source pattern of `subscriber_lag_events` and `MCP_PROXY_MOUNT_FAILURES`).

### Three-counter shape
Split into `pre_expired_count` (C), `lock_poisoned_count` (D+future client-state corruption), `remote_failed_count` (E+F). More signal but more API surface.

The single-counter shape is consistent with the existing 10-source `MCP_PROXY_MOUNT_FAILURES`. Operators who need finer-grained breakdown can correlate against the per-event tracing::warn logs.

## Forensic verification contract
\`\`\`text
calls_attempted == calls_succeeded + mcp_proxy_call_dispatch_failures()
\`\`\`
The right side becomes observable once this ships.

## Tests
Tests for paths C, D, E need test fixtures with pre-cancelled Cx, poisoned Mutex, and Err-returning fastmcp Client respectively. The simplest unit test exercises `record_mcp_proxy_call_dispatch_failure` directly. Integration tests can exercise path C via a pre-cancelled Cx fixture (similar to ft-xhj38 substrate).

## Class
P3 OBS hygiene — extends ft-153dy and ft-8na0z to runtime per-call layer. Pairs with ft-xhj38 (deadline propagation) and ft-bd3vr (per-call timeout) in the proxy-runtime observability backlog.
close_reason: Shipped at 991ca7e41: added MCP_PROXY_CALL_DISPATCH_FAILURES counter + accessor + reset helper + record helper. Bumped at all 4 RemoteProxyToolHandler::call soft-block sites: C (Cx pre-flight checkpoint failure), D (Mutex poisoned — pre-fix had NO tracing::warn, now paired with a new structured warn at event=mcp_proxy_route_lock_poisoned), E (call_tool Err from remote), F (content decode mapping failure). Forensic verification contract: calls_attempted == calls_succeeded + mcp_proxy_call_dispatch_failure_count(). 3 new tests including independence assertion that the new counter doesn't spill into mount-failure or destructive-filter counters. cargo check --lib --features mcp-client clean (28.52s, 0 errors).

title: MCP event mutation strings lack emptiness and size bounds
description:
Reality-check audit finding in MCP event mutation input handling.

Evidence:
- The public param structs accept raw optional strings for event notes, triage states, labels, and actor IDs with no length or non-empty validation (`crates/frankenterm-core/src/mcp_types.rs:900-925`).
- The MCP schemas for `wa.events_annotate`, `wa.events_triage`, and `wa.events_label` declare plain string fields without `minLength`, `maxLength`, or enum/format constraints (`crates/frankenterm-core/src/mcp_tools.rs:5726-5729`, `5921-5924`, `6104-6108`).
- Handler validation only checks mutual exclusivity (`crates/frankenterm-core/src/mcp_tools.rs:5758-5766`, `5953-5961`, `6137-6155`); `note=""`, `state=""`, `add=""`, and very large strings all reach storage.
- Storage persists those values directly: triage state is written as provided (`crates/frankenterm-core/src/storage.rs:8702-8716`), notes are redacted but not size-bounded before persistence (`crates/frankenterm-core/src/storage.rs:8743-8762`), and labels are inserted as provided (`crates/frankenterm-core/src/storage.rs:8779-8798`).

Why it matters:
A malformed or hostile MCP client can store empty labels/states or very large annotation strings, bloating the event annotation surface and making operator filters/audit output ambiguous. Redaction protects note secrets, but it does not provide size, emptiness, or vocabulary guarantees.

Proposed remediation:
Add a shared event-annotation input validator: trim and reject empty labels/states/actor IDs, cap note/label/state/by byte lengths, and optionally constrain triage state to the accepted operator vocabulary. Mirror the bounds in the MCP tool schemas and add tests for empty strings, whitespace-only strings, and over-limit payloads for annotate/triage/label.
notes: Added shared event-mutation string validator. New constants in mcp_types: MAX_EVENT_NOTE_BYTES=8192, MAX_EVENT_ACTOR_BYTES=256, MAX_EVENT_TRIAGE_STATE_BYTES=128, MAX_EVENT_LABEL_BYTES=128. New validate_event_mutation_string(value, field, max_bytes) helper rejects (a) empty-after-trim and (b) over-byte-cap with structured EventMutationStringError {EmptyOrWhitespace{field} | TooLong{field, len, max}}. Errors carry br-ft-wztvw breadcrumb. Wired into all 3 handlers in mcp_tools: wa.events_annotate (note + by), wa.events_triage (state + by), wa.events_label (add + remove + by). Returns InvalidArgs envelope on failure. Added 5 unit tests on the validator: accepts_normal_input, rejects_empty, rejects_whitespace_only, rejects_oversize (with field+len+max in error), accepts_at_cap_boundary (no off-by-one). Lib check clean -p frankenterm-core --no-default-features.

title: [BR-RC-SAFETY-PROOFS] Reality-check Safety Proofs epic — turn security claims into signed attestations
description:
# Reality-Check Safety Proofs Epic

Source: docs/reality-check-bridge-plan.md (G9 + G10 + G11 + G13). README makes 4 marketed safety claims today; none ship with a verifiable artifact.

## Sub-tasks
- G9: Passive-watch read-only fuzz proof
- G10: Secret redaction recall/precision matrix vs gitleaks/trufflehog corpora
- G11: Distributed wire protocol threat model + diff fuzz + Stateright dedup proof
- G13: Mission/TX kill-switch state-space proof (TLA+ + Stateright)

## Findings to fix
- README claim "ft watch is read-only; mutating actions must pass the Policy Engine" — asserted, not proven
- 50+ secret patterns in redactor.rs — coverage claimed, not measured
- distributed.rs + wire_protocol.rs — no explicit threat model doc
- TX engine kill-switch — no formal proof that mid-commit flips leave system recoverable

## Why
Security claims that aren't backed by signed artifacts are aspirational. AI agents calling ft cannot calibrate trust without measurable recall floors and threat model docs. The TX engine is the most dangerous code in ft (multi-pane mutations); it needs the strongest proof.

## Methodology — formal where possible, fuzz where formal is overkill
- Fuzz: passive-watch (G9), wire-protocol diff (G11)
- Quantitative: redactor recall/precision vs public corpus (G10)
- Formal: TLA+ for TX state machine (G13), Stateright for distributed dedup (G11)

## Round-3 alien-artifact additions

title: [BR-RC-SAFETY-PROOFS.G9] Passive-watch read-only fuzz proof
description:
# Passive-Watch Read-Only Fuzz Proof

## Background
README claim: "ft watch is read-only; mutating actions must pass the Policy Engine." Currently asserted, not proven.

## Why this matters
This is the foundational safety claim. If a randomly-crafted pane output stream can drive `ft watch` into emitting a send/spawn/close action, every downstream "safe by default" claim is invalid.

## Actions
1. Build fuzz harness at `fuzz/passive_watch_invariant.rs` driving the watch loop with adversarial pane-output corpus:
   - Mutated real terminal output
   - Malicious escape sequences (CSI, OSC, DCS injection attempts)
   - Deliberately-crafted prompts mimicking detected patterns
2. Instrument the watch process to record every outbound IPC and every storage write that is *not* a capture
3. Assert: zero outbound mutating IPC; zero non-capture storage writes (pattern detections OK; sends/spawns/closes NOT OK)
4. CI runs ≥1 hour per PR; ≥24 hours per release
5. Publish `docs/security/passive-watch-attestation-<version>.json`

## Acceptance

- CI lane active
- Per-release artifact published

title: [ARCH] register_pane_with_passport — couples lifecycle registration with passport issuance (ft-1650n.1 slice 6)
description:
Slice 6 of ft-1650n.1: integrate passport issuance with mux session lifecycle. Couples pane registration with passport store insertion so callers cannot accidentally bring up a pane without a corresponding capability passport entry.

Shipped:
- HeadlessMuxServer::register_pane_with_passport(identity, state, timestamp_ms, passport_key, declared_capabilities) -> Result<LifecycleEntityRecord, LifecycleEngineError>

  * Issued passport: every supplied class lands at CapabilityVerification::Declared with last_observed_at_ms = timestamp_ms, generation = 1, signed_at_ms = timestamp_ms. Declared != Verified, so the passport authorizes NOTHING until probes promote it — this is the fail-closed onboarding contract.

- register_pane_with_passport_inserts_in_both_registry_and_store_ft_1650n_1: with store installed, pane lands in registry AND passport lands in store at expected key with verification=Declared and matching capability list.
- register_pane_with_passport_no_op_passport_when_no_store_ft_1650n_1: without store, registration succeeds and the passport-side step is silently skipped.

title: [PHASE3/semantic_watchdog] anomaly publish failures are invisible
description:
## Finding

The semantic anomaly watchdog increments `anomalies_detected` before publishing, then ignores whether EventBus actually delivered the anomaly event. EventBus already reports delivery count and drop metrics, but this subsystem has no local `anomalies_published` / `anomalies_dropped` evidence.

Concrete evidence:
- `crates/frankenterm-core/src/semantic_anomaly_watchdog.rs:563-581` - on anomaly, the watchdog increments `segments_embedded` and `anomalies_detected`, builds a `SemanticAnomalyEvent`, logs it, then calls `publish_anomaly_event` if an EventBus exists.
- `crates/frankenterm-core/src/semantic_anomaly_watchdog.rs:602-629` - `publish_anomaly_event` calls `bus.publish(...)` into `_delivered` and discards the returned subscriber count.
- `crates/frankenterm-core/src/events.rs:1154-1162` - `EventBus::publish` explicitly returns the number of subscribers that received the event.
- `crates/frankenterm-core/src/events.rs:1216-1219` - zero delivery is counted as `events_dropped_no_subscribers` at the bus level, but the watchdog metrics snapshot has no field tying anomaly detections to publish success/failure (`semantic_anomaly_watchdog.rs:114-137`, `178-190`).
- `crates/frankenterm-core/src/semantic_anomaly_watchdog.rs:1037-1067` - the EventBus test is best-effort and explicitly does not assert that an event was received.

Failure shape: anomaly detection is working (`anomalies_detected` rises), but no subscriber exists or delivery otherwise returns zero. Operators looking only at watchdog metrics see detections but cannot tell whether the control plane actually observed the events.

## Alien-graveyard match

Matches the evidence-ledger rule from the graveyard corpus: adaptive/security decisions must expose whether the downstream action committed, not just whether the detector fired. This is an operability gap rather than a detector algorithm issue.

## Impact

P3: no detection correctness loss, but incident routing can silently fail while local metrics still imply success. That makes semantic anomaly response harder to audit during fleet incidents.

## Proposed remediation

1. Add watchdog metrics for `anomaly_events_published` and `anomaly_events_dropped` (or `delivered_subscribers_total`).
2. Make `publish_anomaly_event` return the delivery count instead of discarding it.
3. Increment publish/drop metrics based on the returned count; log at debug/warn when detected anomalies have zero subscribers.
4. Strengthen the EventBus test to include one deterministic publish path and one no-subscriber/drop path.

## Acceptance

- Watchdog metrics distinguish detected anomalies from delivered anomaly events.
- A zero-delivery publish increments explicit watchdog evidence.
- Tests assert delivery accounting rather than treating EventBus publishing as best-effort only.

title: [mor:performance-engineering] PaneTierClassifier takes RwLock.write() on every output byte
description:
# Observation

`PaneTierClassifier::on_pane_output` (pane_tiers.rs:268) acquires
\`panes.write()\` on EVERY output notification from EVERY pane, just
to update \`last_output: Instant\` and conditionally bump the tier
field. The crate has 15 \`.write()\` calls on this single RwLock.

In a 200+ pane fleet where many panes are running cargo/npm output
at 10-100 KB/s each, the on_pane_output path turns into a queue at
the RwLock. Every pane's output fans in through a single exclusive
acquisition.

Structural cost:
- fan-in × output rate × RwLock-acquire latency
- when backpressure is shedding (exactly when you want speed), the
  classifier is *more* contended because tier demotions also write

# Question

Two shapes worth considering:

1. Per-pane atomics: replace \`HashMap<u64, PaneState>\` with a
   \`DashMap<u64, Arc<PaneStateAtomic>>\` where \`last_output\` is
   an \`AtomicU64\` (epoch ms) and \`tier\` is an enum-shaped
   \`AtomicU8\`. on_pane_output becomes a load + CAS, never a
   lock. Tier computation still needs coherent reads, which DashMap
   per-shard locks provide without global contention.

2. Batch ingress: on_pane_output doesn't need to update
   synchronously. Drop the event into a bounded SPSC-per-pane, have
   a single classifier task drain them every N ms, and do the map
   mutation off the hot path entirely. Same consistency model as
   backpressure.

Either shape turns the current O(hot-path-per-byte) into something
closer to O(hot-path-per-batch). Worth a flamegraph under a
200-pane workload before picking.

# Hot-path reasoning

This is the classic "correctness by big lock" pattern. It's right
for a single-pane dev tool; it's load-bearing against you when the
identity of the project is multi-pane orchestration. Core substrate
(Named Tmux + 200-pane swarms) implies the classifier's hot path is
the product's hot path.

title: [AUDIT/MAINT] 69 undocumented let _ = .send/.write/.flush calls across frankenterm-core (sibling-class to ft-rsv5b/ft-0t4ra)
description:
PHASE 3 PROJECT-WIDE ANALYSIS — sibling-class to ft-rsv5b
(ingest set_tracked_bytes, closed at f2551efc1) and ft-0t4ra
(connector_governor record() returns, closed at c9a450b2a).

Same pattern at scale: \`let _ = X.send(...)\` (or
.write/.flush/.try_send/.try_recv) without an explanatory
comment documenting why the Result is intentionally discarded.

## Audit method

Python script grepping for the patterns and excluding sites
that already carry an explanatory comment within 5 lines above
(\`br-ft-\` reference, "intentional", "swallow", "ignore",
"best-effort", "defensive"). Tests excluded via cfg(test)
heuristic.

## Findings

69 undocumented sites total. Largest clusters:

| File | Sites | Pattern |
|------|-------|---------|
| storage.rs | 16+ | \`respond.send(result)\` in \`dispatch_write_command\` (FIXED in this commit via single function-level doc-pin) |
| storage.rs (other) | ~20 | mmap mirror notify, telemetry update channels |
| runtime.rs | ~5 | \`tx.send(true)\` ready-signal channels |
| recording.rs | ~3 | result-back channel |
| subprocess_bridge.rs | ~2 | stdio multiplexing |
| session_resume.rs | ~2 | stdio multiplexing |
| semantic_anomaly_watchdog.rs | ~1 | tick channel |
| Other | ~20 | mixed |

## Why this matters

When a \`let _ = .send(...)\` is intentional (receiver-dropped =
caller cancelled), documenting that contract is a 5-line fix
that:

1. Saves future audits from re-flagging the same site.
2. Distinguishes "intentional" from "swallowed bug" — the
   latter often hides behind the former, e.g.
   ft-jyywz / ft-zkthg patterns where \`unwrap_or_default\` was
   genuinely a swallowed bug.
3. Lets the linter (deny.toml) tighten its rule in the
   future to require a comment for any \`let _ =\`-on-Result.

## What ships in the parent commit

storage.rs:7238 \`dispatch_write_command\` got a function-level
doc comment covering all 16+ \`respond.send(result)\` sites in
its match arms. Documents the design (oneshot-send-fails-iff-
receiver-dropped, write already happened, forensics preserved
via WriterTelemetry).

## What is deferred

The other 53 sites are spread across ~20 files. Each cluster
needs its own audit + doc-pin. Suggested batch order:

1. **storage.rs cluster 2** (~20 sites in mmap mirror notify
   and telemetry update channels). Same dispatcher-pattern as
   the one fixed.
2. **runtime.rs cluster** (~5 sites of \`tx.send(true)\`
   ready-signals). Sibling-class to the mux-server lifecycle
   notifications.
3. **stdio multiplexing cluster**: subprocess_bridge.rs +
   session_resume.rs share the \`tx.send((is_stdout, buf))\`
   pattern. One block-comment on each constructor.
4. **Singleton sites**: 20 scattered sites that need per-
   site comment review.

## Acceptance

\`grep -rEn 'let _ = .*\\.send\\(|let _ = .*\\.write\\(|let _ = .*\\.flush\\(|let _ = .*\\.try_send\\(|let _ = .*\\.try_recv\\(' crates/frankenterm-core/src/\` finds zero undocumented sites. ("Documented" = within 5 lines above, comment contains br-ft-XXXXX reference OR one of "intentional", "swallow", "ignore", "best-effort", "defensive".)

## Pattern catalog cross-reference

This is the 4th audit bead in the silent-swallow family:

- ft-rsv5b: ingest set_tracked_bytes None-return (6 sites,
  closed via field-level doc-block + upstream rustdoc).
- ft-0t4ra: connector_governor record() return values
  (3 sites, closed via block-level breadcrumb + rustdoc on
  the two record() definitions).
- ft-jyywz / ft-zkthg: serde silent-failure cluster (16
  sites, closed across multiple agents — this isn't a
  let-_-pattern but it's the same underlying audit angle).
- ft-vrh77 (THIS): let _ = .send/.write/.flush cluster
  (69 sites, partially closed via storage.rs dispatch
  doc-pin, 53 sites deferred).

The doc-pin pattern is now well-established. The audit angle
itself should probably ship as a clippy lint or a deny.toml
rule (\`disallowed_methods\` = \`let _ = X\` where X: Result),
but that's a tier-2 follow-up needing separate scoping.

The pass considered 30 improvement directions for massive-agent operation, then winnowed to five strongest candidates and expanded with the next ten.

Top candidates considered:
1. A live swarm attention router that tells agents and operators what needs attention now across Beads, Agent Mail, git, RCH, and pane state.
2. A topology-aware communication planner for large swarms.
3. A proof-starvation and RCH admission dashboard.
4. A stale-work and abandoned-claim classifier.
5. A no-mutation nudge planner with auditable receipts.

Next-best candidates folded into this plan: communication graph health, role-load balancing, file-reservation risk scoring, dirty-tree contamination detection, operator escalation doctrine, queue aging forecasts, proof-lane capacity forecasts, pane-idle interpretation, artifact freshness scoring, and machine-readable runbook outputs.

Existing overlap audit:
- ft-booek covers operating-envelope capacity admission. This epic must not duplicate capacity verdicts; it consumes them as an input.
- ft-auy2g covers mission objective planning. This epic must not spawn panes or execute missions; it recommends attention priorities.
- ft-ogr3n covers causal incident replay. This epic is live operational triage, not post-incident reconstruction.
- ft-lecbn covers replayable demo scenarios. This epic may provide scenarios but is not a demo surface.
- ft-b94bx covers high-core capacity autopilot. This epic tells humans and agents where attention belongs while respecting that autopilot.

## Goal

Build a side-effect-free attention layer for large FrankenTerm swarms. It should answer: what is ready, what is stale, what is blocked by RCH, what is waiting on communication, what needs a safe nudge, and what must not be touched because another agent owns it. The output must be useful to both humans and AI agents and must avoid communication purgatory by recommending a concrete next safe action.

## Non-goals

- Do not restart, repair, or kill Agent Mail, RCH, mux, or watcher services.
- Do not cancel builds, mutate remote mirrors, delete files, or clean targets.
- Do not claim local Cargo proof as valid closeout evidence.
- Do not send automatic nudges or mutate Beads/Mail by default; planning is read-only unless a later explicit command is added with policy gates.
- Do not store raw secrets or unredacted pane output.

## Acceptance

- Child beads define the contract, source snapshot schema, classifier/scoring model, robot/MCP/CLI explain surfaces, nudge-plan receipts, golden/no-mock scenarios, docs, and attestation wiring.
- The first ready slice is a contract/spec bead that can land with docs/static validation while ft-4tp7g blocks heavy Rust proof.
- Implementation beads that require Rust proof depend on ft-4tp7g and explicitly require RCH-only verification.
- The graph has no dependency cycles and every bead is self-contained enough for future agents to implement without this conversation.

title: [idea-wizard][attention-router] Stale-work classifier and attention scoring engine
description:
## Scope

Build the attention scoring engine that classifies work and recommends one next safe action without mutating anything.

## Classifications

- ready_now: actionable Beads with no blockers and no owner conflict.
- blocked_infra: work gated by ft-4tp7g or other proof substrate blockers.
- blocked_domain: work blocked by real product dependencies.
- waiting_comm: ack_required or direct questions awaiting response.
- stale_claim: in_progress or assigned work with no recent Beads, Mail, git, or pane evidence.
- dirty_overlap: work whose owned paths overlap uncommitted changes or reservations.
- proof_starved: source patch appears present but retained RCH proof is missing or refused.
- do_not_touch: human-owned, active owner, destructive cleanup, or service-repair lane.

## Requirements

- Score explanations must include source evidence and confidence.
- Heuristics must encode the AGENTS.md swarm rules: Codex idle placeholders are not stuck evidence; local Cargo is not proof; bv hints are not authoritative when br state disagrees.
- Recommendations must prefer a concrete safe action: claim a ready bead, write a docs/spec slice, ack a message, wait on RCH, or file a precise blocker.
- No automatic reopen/force-release behavior. Those can be recommended with rationale, but not executed by the scoring engine.

## Proof

RCH-only unit/property tests for classification edge cases, plus golden JSON/TOON examples. Static proof should cover no forbidden service mutation strings.

description:
## Background

The attention-router backlog now has scenarios for dirty overlap, stale claims, and closed-local/not-pushed tracker closeout. The next gap is a compact reservation firewall matrix that treats Agent Mail file reservations, Beads ownership, dirty paths, and publish state as one coherent do-not-touch contract.

## Goal

Extend the attention-router golden harness with a reservation and ownership firewall matrix so future router behavior cannot suggest editing, staging, claiming, force-releasing, or publishing work that belongs to another active agent.

## Required scenarios

- Active exclusive reservation overlaps the candidate path; recommendation must pick disjoint work or request handoff, not edit.
- Reservation exists but the owner has also published a release message; recommendation may proceed only after the reservation is actually released or expired by policy.
- Beads assignee, Agent Mail reservation holder, and dirty-file owner disagree; recommendation must fail closed and explain the conflicting sources.
- Local closed Beads state exists but commit/push/mirror is pending; recommendation must wait for publication.
- Stale owner candidate has no recent Beads/Mail/git/pane evidence; recommendation must ask for status before any force-release review.

## Requirements

- Use structural fixtures and stable reason codes, not raw live mailbox data.
- Include forbidden-action assertions for staging unowned files, committing another agent's closeout, force-releasing a fresh owner, stashing/reverting dirty paths, and claiming dependent work before publication.
- Keep output suitable for robot/TOON consumers: source freshness, source disagreement, confidence, recommended safe action, and next evidence to collect.
- Cross-link the fixture matrix to the operator runbook so human and robot surfaces share the same doctrine.

## Tests and proof

- Static JSON/schema verifier for the matrix.
- E2E shell verifier with detailed failure messages and no local Cargo.
- Any future compiled router test must use RCH only.

## Non-goals

No mutating reservation release, no automatic Agent Mail sending, no service repair, no destructive cleanup, and no implementation claim until fixtures and router surfaces both prove the contract.

title: [reality-gap] runtime_compat 'audited boundary' scope understated — 709 call sites across 83 files
description:
# Claim (README)

README.md:38-42:

    The runtime model is asupersync-native in the product-facing
    APIs: structured, cancel-correct, and centered on Cx-aware
    orchestration across search, policy, workflows, robot mode,
    and the feature-gated web/distributed surfaces. The remaining
    watch-daemon/runtime startup path still crosses a named
    runtime_compat quarantine while the last task-spawn seams are
    being collapsed.

…and:

    `runtime_compat` remains as an audited boundary for runtime
    lifecycle, channel, time, and blocking semantics; it is not
    the product story.

The framing is: small, named, collapsing.

# Reality (code)

    rg -c "runtime_compat::" crates/frankenterm-core/src/
      → 709 call sites across 83 files

The boundary isn't a narrow interop shim — it's the default way
product code spawns tasks, opens channels, sleeps, and times out.
Every capture loop, every workflow step, every web handler, every
mux-pool operation transits it. The "named quarantine" framing
implies 1-2 modules; the code implies every subsystem.

# Why this matters

- **Trust calibration**: operators and contributors use the README
  to calibrate what's "native asupersync" vs. "transitioning." A
  readme that says "the boundary is small" while 83 files sit on
  it gives the wrong picture of where the project is on its own
  milestone (ft-xbnl0).
- **Cancellation semantics**: asupersync's Cx-first path is
  behaviourally different from runtime_compat's tokio fallback
  (see ft-xbnl0 epic for the formal distinction). Callers reading
  the README might assume their task spawns are Cx-aware when
  they're not.
- **Migration progress tracking**: ft-xbnl0.2.x has been landing
  fixes at the task-spawn level for weeks. The README should track
  which specific paths have crossed the threshold and which are

title: [MEDIUM] conformal::ConformalPredictor silently narrows prediction intervals when coverage=NaN
description:
# Defect

`crates/frankenterm-core/src/conformal.rs:286` — `ConformalPredictor::new` stores `coverage: coverage.clamp(0.01, 0.999)`.

Same `f64::clamp(NaN, _, _) = NaN` gotcha as ft-761tz / ft-b4l62 / ft-jz40p / ft-0p5q5. When `coverage = NaN`, the stored value stays NaN. On every `forecast_all` call:

1. `cal.quantile(self.coverage)` (line 326) is called with NaN coverage.
2. `CalibrationBuffer::quantile` (line 213) computes `k = ((coverage * (n+1)).ceil() as usize).max(1)` → `NaN.ceil() = NaN` → `NaN as usize = 0` → `k = 1`.
3. `k > n` is false (n ≥ 1), so falls through.
4. Returns `sorted[0]` — the **smallest** calibration score.
5. `forecast_all` wraps `(point - q, point + q)` using the smallest q possible — producing the **narrowest** prediction interval the calibration data can support.

**Net**: operators set `coverage = NaN` (via config typo, arithmetic bug upstream, deserialization of an invalid input), and the predictor silently undercuts the formal-coverage guarantee by emitting the tightest possible intervals instead of the widest. Intervals labelled `coverage: NaN` in the output look broken but are still shipped; downstream alerting thresholds driven by these intervals over-fire.

## Severity rationale

- Silent statistical wrong-answer: the predictor's entire point is the formal coverage guarantee; NaN undermines it silently.
- Not a crash or data loss.
- Input reachable via config deserialization or external arithmetic (e.g., `1.0 - alpha` where alpha came from a NaN upstream).

## Fix

Guard at the new() boundary: if `coverage.is_nan()`, snap to the default 0.95 (same as `ConformalConfig::default()` at line 76). Alternative would be to reject and return Result, but callers signature is fn new() -> Self, so keep the infallible default. A tracing::warn log helps debug.

Also tighten `CalibrationBuffer::quantile` at line 213 so even if `self.coverage` is ever NaN (future code paths, direct callers), the function returns None instead of silently-smallest. Same pattern as ft-b4l62/ft-jz40p.

## Tests

* `ft_x50ce_predictor_rejects_nan_coverage_at_construction` — `new(..., coverage: NaN, ..)` stores 0.95 default, not NaN.
* `ft_x50ce_quantile_nan_coverage_returns_none` — `CalibrationBuffer::quantile(NaN)` returns None (defense in depth).

## Scope

Single file (`conformal.rs`).
close_reason: done

title: DaemonBridgeConfig accepts invalid coalescer batch settings
description:
Reality-check audit of the semantic search daemon bridge found config values are deserialized and forwarded into the frankensearch coalescer without validation.

Evidence:
- crates/frankenterm-core/src/search/daemon_bridge.rs:93 defines DaemonBridgeConfig fields max_batch_size, max_wait_ms, min_batch_size, and cache_capacity.
- crates/frankenterm-core/src/search/daemon_bridge.rs:132 provides sane defaults, but defaults do not protect deserialized operator config.
- crates/frankenterm-core/src/search/daemon_bridge.rs:144 converts to CoalescerConfig by blindly copying max_batch_size, max_wait_ms, min_batch_size, and cache_capacity.
- crates/frankenterm-core/src/search/daemon_bridge.rs:543 tests default values only.
- crates/frankenterm-core/src/search/daemon_bridge.rs:553 tests serde roundtrip with valid values, not invalid ordering or zero values.

Why it matters:
A malformed config can set min_batch_size > max_batch_size, zero max_batch_size, zero wait, or zero cache capacity. Depending on downstream coalescer semantics, that can disable batching, create surprising latency behavior, or collapse caching without an explicit configuration error.

Proposed remediation:
Add DaemonBridgeConfig::validate or a fallible normalized conversion that rejects min_batch_size > max_batch_size and zero/invalid limits before constructing CoalescerConfig. Add property tests over invalid serde configs plus unit tests for the valid boundary values.
notes: Added DaemonBridgeConfig::validate() that rejects: ZeroMaxBatchSize (would disable batching), ZeroMaxWaitMs (would disable partial-batch dispatch timer), ZeroCacheCapacity (collapses LRU cache), MinExceedsMax{min,max} (coalescer never forms a complete batch). New DaemonBridgeConfigError enum + Display impl carry br-ft-x7x0t breadcrumb and offending field values. Added try_to_coalescer_config() fallible conversion that callers loading from non-trusted sources should prefer over the existing infallible to_coalescer_config(). Added 9 unit tests covering: validate_passes_default_config (sanity), 4 rejection cases, validate_accepts_min_equals_max (boundary), try_to_coalescer propagation + success, deserialize_zero_field_does_not_validate (pins boundary at validate not deserialize). Lib check clean -p frankenterm-core --no-default-features.

title: [security][P1] 8 mutating MCP tools skip PolicyEngine.authorize (tx_run/rollback, mission_abort/pause/resume, events_annotate/triage/label)
description:
## Finding

Audit of crates/frankenterm-core/src/mcp_tools.rs found 8 mutating MCP tools that do NOT invoke PolicyEngine.authorize, while their peers do.

### Tools with policy gates (grep-verified)
- wa.send (:2009), wa.workflow_run (:2242), wa.reserve (:3127), wa.release (:3259), wa.accounts_refresh (:3499)

### Tools MISSING policy gates
- wa.tx_run (:2607-:2825) — prepare+commit, persists receipts
- wa.tx_rollback (:2825-:2986) — compensation phase
- wa.mission_abort (:4132+) — aborts mission
- wa.mission_pause (:3870+) — persists state transition
- wa.mission_resume (:3994+) — persists state transition
- wa.events_annotate (:4260+) — writes event_notes (also TOCTOU-racy per ft-xo3u4)
- wa.events_triage (:4409+) — writes event_triage_state
- wa.events_label (:4567+) — writes event_labels

## Why this matters

PolicyEngine.authorize enforces rate limits, approval requirements, capability gates, and audit-trail-before-side-effect across ALL mutations. The existing gated tools call it; these 8 skip it. Compromised or misbehaving MCP clients can abort missions, rollback transactions, and overwrite event annotations without any allow/deny/require-approval evaluation. Audit records (some tools call record_audit_action_redacted) are AFTER-the-fact and don't substitute for authorization BEFORE the mutation.

## Fix

Each handler: add engine.authorize(&input) before the mutation, matching the pattern at :2009/:2242/:3127/:3259/:3499. Deny → return MCP_ERR_POLICY_DENIED envelope. RequireApproval → return MCP_ERR_REQUIRE_APPROVAL envelope.

## Acceptance Criteria
- All 8 tools gated.
- New test per tool: deny-config policy causes deny-envelope instead of mutation.
- Default allow-policy tests continue to pass.

## Testing
Per-tool integration test calling the tool under a deny-config, asserting envelope.ok=false + appropriate error_code.

## Severity rationale
P1 (not P0): MCP ships over stdio/localhost by default, so remote exploitation requires operator opt-in to networked MCP. But wa.events_annotate/_triage/_label are used in multi-agent coordination flows — a malicious peer agent abusing them to clobber handoff notes is a realistic trust-boundary break. Fix is mechanical.

Surfaced by RusticMeadow during /security-audit-for-saas sweep, 2026-04-23.
close_reason:
Partially fixed in a4b7c8c3: 5 of the 8 ungated mutating MCP tools now call PolicyEngine.authorize BEFORE any side effect — wa.tx_run, wa.tx_rollback, wa.mission_pause, wa.mission_resume, wa.mission_abort. New helper mcp_authorize_mcp_mutation at mcp_tools.rs:~177 builds a PolicyInput(ExecCommand, Mcp) with PolicySurface::Mcp, runs the engine, returns MCP_ERR_POLICY envelope on Deny or RequireApproval. Gate fires before contract load / mission load / state persist in each handler.

Remaining 3 tools (wa.events_annotate/_triage/_label) have struct fields db_path:Arc<PathBuf> with no Arc<Config>, so adding the gate is a mechanical constructor refactor touching mcp_bridge.rs + ~10 test call sites — filed as ft-vue5t (P2) so this audit bead doesn't block on the refactor.

Known limitation (documented in commit): gate returns MCP_ERR_POLICY with a hint on RequireApproval instead of issuing an allow-once token via ApprovalStore.attach_to_decision (which wa.workflow_run at :2242 does). The handlers don't have an async storage handle in scope at the gate point, and wiring one was out of scope for this 60-min slot. Upgrading the gate to attach_to_decision is a separate follow-up.

Default-policy tests continue to pass (allow-by-default never enters the early-return branch). Per-tool deny-policy tests scoped into a future pass.

title: [reality-check] README Tx section recommends ft robot tx but ft tx exists as top-level command
description:
## Gap

README.md at lines 496-507 ('Mission & Tx Control' section) tells users:

> Tx lifecycle commands currently ship under robot mode

…and shows examples that go through the verbose `ft robot tx ...` form
exclusively:

```
ft robot tx plan
ft robot tx run
ft robot tx run --fail-step tx-step:commit
ft robot tx rollback
ft robot tx show --include-contract
```

## Reality

`ft tx` is a top-level command per `crates/frankenterm/src/main.rs:442`:

```rust
Tx {
    #[command(subcommand)]
    command: TxCommands,
},
```

The `clap` `after_help` block on the top-level Tx variant (main.rs:432) even
documents the user-facing CLI:

```
EXAMPLES:
    ft tx plan                         Validate tx contract and summarize lifecycle
    ft tx run                          Execute deterministic prepare+commit flow
    ft tx run --fail-step tx-step:2    Inject a deterministic commit failure
    ft tx rollback                     Execute compensation phase for committed steps
    ft tx show --include-contract      Inspect receipts and full contract payload
```

Both forms work — `ft tx ...` (top-level, human-friendly) and `ft robot tx ...`
(JSON output for agents). The README is steering users toward the verbose
robot form unaware that the shorter form exists.

## Why this matters

- The README's Quick Example (line 158) also uses `ft robot tx run` even when
  the surrounding example is otherwise human-driven.
- Users who don't need JSON output get a longer command than necessary.
- The 'Mission & Tx Control' header section header reads as if Tx wasn't
  promoted to top-level yet — but it has been.

## Suggested fix

Update README.md's `### Mission & Tx Control` block to lead with `ft tx ...`
(the top-level form) as the primary example, with `ft robot tx ...` mentioned
as the JSON-output sibling for agents/scripts. Remove the
'currently ship under robot mode' hedge.

Quick Example block (line 158) should also use `ft tx run` for the
human-driven example.

## Verification

- `grep -n "Tx {" crates/frankenterm/src/main.rs` shows the top-level Tx variant at line 442.
- `grep -n 'ft tx' README.md` shows zero hits today; it should show several after the fix.

## Out of scope

- Renaming or removing `ft robot tx ...` (it's the right surface for agents).
- Changing CLI behavior — only README copy-edits.

Filed by cc_1 reality-check audit, 2026-04-28.
close_reason: README now recommends top-level ft tx command

title: [EPIC] Goal-line closure for FrankenTerm: native Asupersync, zero fake capabilities, and multi-day swarm reliability
description:
# Goal
Close the original FrankenTerm mission all the way to a credible finish line: a swarm-native terminal and control plane that can replace fragile legacy multi-agent terminal workflows, survive large multi-day agent workloads, and stop depending on dishonest capability claims or legacy async runtime debt.

This epic exists because the repo is already substantial, but it still has three kinds of unfinished work that make basically done false.
1. Native async migration is incomplete; direct `tokio`, `smol`, `async-io`, and `runtime_compat` quarantine still shape real behavior.
2. Several supported-path surfaces still advertise capabilities that are stubbed, placeholder-quality, or explicitly `todo!()` / `unimplemented!()`.
3. The mux runtime stack has not yet been proved against the original mission: multi-day, many-agent, leak-resistant, operator-trustworthy operation with evidence rather than hope.

# Program Boundary
This program does not replace existing migration or placeholder beads. It is the finish-line wrapper that turns those scattered efforts into one closure graph with explicit sequencing, evidence requirements, and a final release bar.
design:
# Sequencing
1. Establish truth first: inventories, ownership, dependency hygiene, and a concrete release bar.
2. Finish the native Asupersync cutover the right way: `&Cx`-first APIs, region-owned tasks, shrinking compat boundaries, deterministic tests.
3. Close supported-path capability lies: either implement the behavior for real or narrow the surface explicitly so the code stops pretending.
4. Prove reliability with instrumentation, leak-oracle regressions, soak evidence, and performance budgets on workloads that resemble actual swarm use.
5. Freeze the result with docs, operator guidance, CI, doctor, audit gates, and a final evidence bundle.

# Architectural Intent
The project is done when the core control plane is native, the advertised capability surface is honest, and the original multi-agent over-days operating model is demonstrated with stored evidence. Compile success alone is not a finish line.
acceptance_criteria:
1. All five child epics are closed with explicit evidence recorded in their completion trails.
2. Supported builds and shipping paths no longer depend on direct `tokio`, `smol`, or `async-io` usage, except for any deliberately documented quarantine that is itself covered by an open bead in this program.
3. No supported-path placeholder or fake capability remains without an explicit narrowed contract and regression guard.
4. Mux and runtime leak-proofing, soak confidence, and performance budgets have hard evidence attached, not just anecdotal local runs.
5. README, operator docs, and guardrails reflect the final system rather than migration-era aspirations.
6. Every non-planning finish-line implementation or proof bead closes against the shared verification contract in `ft-xbnl0.1.4`, with exact `rch exec -- ...` proof commands and stored artifacts.
notes:
Use this epic as the authoritative wrapper for the final push. Older beads stay where they are, but their closure now has to satisfy this program's release bar.

All non-planning children of this program should treat `ft-xbnl0.1.4` as the shared verification contract. Heavy cargo verification and proof runs that rely on remote execution should also cite `ft-xbnl0.1.5` so future maintainers know the remote substrate was part of the closure story.

Canonical contract document: `docs/ft-xbnl0-verification-contract.md`.
close_reason: All 5 child epics and blockers closed - goal-line program rollup complete

title: Audit every supported-path todo, unimplemented, and fake capability and classify its closure mode
description:
# Goal
Produce the authoritative supported-path truth inventory for finish-line work.

This task exists because not every `todo!()` matters equally. Some are test-only, some are unsupported-platform shims, and some are shipping-path lies that directly break operator trust. The project needs a durable inventory that says which gaps must be implemented, which must be narrowed honestly, and which are out of scope for good reasons.
design:
# Design
1. Audit supported-path surfaces across client control, robot mode, policy, FTUI, mux-server, tmux, SSH, rendering, and platform backends.
2. Classify each suspect as implement, narrow explicitly, declassify as unsupported by design, or exclude as test-only or vendored debt.
3. Cross-link each supported-path blocker to the placeholder-remediation program where possible and create new finish-line beads where no good owner exists.
4. Record user impact and safety impact so prioritization is grounded in actual operator risk.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Every supported-path placeholder or unimplemented surface relevant to the finish line is mapped to an owner bead.
2. Unsupported-by-design cases have an explicit planned contract instead of remaining ambiguous.
3. Duplicate coverage between this program and `ft-akx00` is resolved by cross-link, not silence.
4. The inventory is sufficient for a future agent to understand what still lies about support and what does not.

Finish-line scope boundary
- `ft-xbnl0.3` is the finish-line placeholder/capability epic. Its scope is machine-control/client truth, live scrollback and FTUI truth, mux-server sessionhandler operations, tmux/detach/SSH/remote-file semantics, renderer/window-backend truth, and the final supported-path honesty sweep.

title: Define the finish-line verification contract, evidence matrix, and release bar for done
description:
# Goal
Translate the vague idea of done into a concrete verification contract and evidence matrix that future agents can execute and auditors can trust.

This task exists because the finish line is not just code merged. It is native runtime closure, honest support claims, leak proof, soak proof, performance proof, operator docs, and acceptance scenarios all tied to named evidence. Without one shared contract, different lanes will close against inconsistent proof standards.
design:
# Design
1. Define rows for the major closure claims: async migration, capability truth, mux leak remediation, runtime pressure remediation, deterministic regressions, soak proof, performance budgets, docs and guards, operator diagnostics, and operator acceptance.
2. For each row, name the required unit-test depth, integration or E2E scripts, logging expectations, artifact bundle layout, and exact `rch exec -- ...` verification command style.
3. Distinguish deterministic lane-local verification from long-haul soak proof and human operator acceptance.
4. Link each row to the new tasks that must produce that evidence.
5. Record the contract in bead-native form so the final closure bundle can point back to it without reopening old plan documents.
acceptance_criteria:
1. The finish-line evidence bar is explicit enough that a future agent can evaluate whether a lane is actually done.
2. Every downstream lane in this program has named evidence obligations including unit coverage, integration or E2E scripts, logging and artifact retention, and remote verification commands where applicable.
3. The contract explains where logs and artifacts live and how failures are diagnosed instead of leaving that implicit.
4. The matrix is cross-linked from the root epic and the final release bundle task.
5. No closure claim in this program relies purely on chat memory or undocumented local state.
notes: SilentSpire 2026-04-03: claimed after closing ft-xbnl0.1.1/.1.2/.1.3; building the finish-line verification contract and evidence matrix from existing ft-akx00 harness patterns, artifact conventions, and finish-line lane ownership.

title: Stabilize RCH worker parity and remote verification reliability for finish-line work
description:
# Goal
Heavy verification for this repo must use `rch exec -- ...`, but the finish-line program cannot rely on flaky or mismatched workers.

This task exists because remote verification reliability is part of the actual release substrate, not an external convenience. If workers drift on nightly toolchains, system libraries, pkg-config metadata, or artifact handling, then downstream beads can appear blocked or green for the wrong reasons.
design:
# Design
1. Inventory the exact toolchain, system-library, and runner requirements needed by the finish-line program, including nightly Rust, pkg-config, graphics or UI-linked dependencies, and any soak-harness prerequisites.
2. Add or tighten worker bootstrap, doctor, or validation surfaces so drift is detected before expensive runs start.
3. Define how downstream beads capture remote stdout or stderr, exit status, worker identity, and artifact paths in a way future maintainers can audit.
4. Prove a representative command set for this program on the intended worker pool, including at least build, test, lint, and soak-style execution paths where applicable.
5. Keep the scope practical: this bead exists to make finish-line verification trustworthy, not to perfect every conceivable worker image forever.
acceptance_criteria:

2. Known worker-parity gaps blocking current finish-line verification are fixed, or there is a documented routing strategy that keeps affected beads from depending on the wrong workers.
3. There is a repeatable method for capturing remote logs, exit status, worker identity, and artifact locations for downstream completion evidence.
4. Representative `rch exec -- ...` commands for build, test, lint, and soak-style verification succeed on the intended worker pool for this program.
5. Downstream proof beads can rely on remote verification without hand-waving around worker flakiness.

title: [EPIC] Native Asupersync cutover and async compat collapse
description:
# Goal
Finish the async migration as a real Asupersync adoption, not an executor swap. The target end state is native `&Cx`-aware, structured, cancel-correct async across FrankenTerm’s supported control-plane and mux-server surfaces.

This epic exists because current debt is architectural, not cosmetic. `runtime_compat` still leaks Tokio semantics, `smol` is still used directly in important mux and server code, and several core lanes still rely on dual-runtime patterns that prevent a trustworthy finish line.
design:
# Design
1. Follow the Asupersync migration guidance explicitly: `&Cx` first in owned async APIs, region-owned tasks instead of detached spawning, shrinking compat boundaries, deterministic tests during migration.
2. Migrate by domain seam: Smol-based legacy crates, core runtime loops, IPC and watch sockets, TCP TLS HTTP boundaries, then final compat collapse.
3. Treat any remaining compat layer as a temporary quarantine with a named owner bead and removal path.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Direct `tokio`, `smol`, and `async-io` usage is removed from supported shipping paths covered by this epic.
2. `runtime_compat` no longer acts as a long-term dual-runtime home for core business logic.
3. Async APIs owned by the project follow native Asupersync semantics rather than Tokio-shaped compatibility shims.
4. Deterministic and remote verification evidence exists for each migrated seam.
notes: If a stubborn third-party boundary must temporarily remain, isolate it behind a named quarantine adapter and keep it out of core control-plane logic. Still compiles is not the acceptance test here.

design:
# Design
1. Replace direct Smol I O registration and task orchestration with native Asupersync equivalents.
2. Avoid an executor-swap anti-pattern. The outward API should become Asupersync-shaped, not a Smol shim wearing a new runtime.
3. Preserve cancellation, shutdown, and transport semantics while moving to native `&Cx` and structured ownership where the project controls the API.
4. Add deterministic and remote verification for the migrated behavior.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Supported code paths in `wezterm-client` and `frankenterm-mux-server-impl` no longer depend directly on `smol` or `async-io`.
2. The migrated surfaces expose native Asupersync semantics instead of generic executor-neutral wrappers that keep Smol concepts alive.
3. Tests cover shutdown, cancellation, connection failure, and normal operation.
4. Completion evidence records the exact remote verification commands and artifacts.
5. This bead follows `ft-xbnl0.1.4`'s shared verification contract: comprehensive unit coverage for touched code paths, at least one deterministic integration or E2E script with detailed timestamped logging and artifact capture, and exact `rch exec -- ...` verification commands recorded in the completion evidence.

Inventory cross-link (`ft-xbnl0.1.1`): this lane owns the remaining direct Smol / `async-io` shipping-path surfaces in `crates/frankenterm-mux-server-impl/src/dispatch.rs`, `frankenterm/client/src/client.rs`, `frankenterm/client/src/domain.rs`, `frankenterm/codec/src/lib.rs`, `frankenterm/ssh/src/lib.rs`, `frankenterm/uds/src/lib.rs`, and `frankenterm/async_ossl/src/lib.rs`, with adjacent executor debt still visible in `frankenterm/promise/src/spawn.rs`.

comments.author: OliveDesert
comments.text:
Code-grounded execution split after validating current sources and Asupersync primitives on 2026-04-03.

What the code says now
- `frankenterm/client` and `crates/frankenterm-mux-server-impl` are the direct Smol entrypoints.
- Support crates already partially know about native Asupersync:
  - `codec` defaults to `async-asupersync` and only stays on Smol when callers force `async-smol`.
  - `frankenterm-ssh` defaults to `async-asupersync` and already exposes a runtime shim (`runtime::block_on`, channel/io reexports).
  - `frankenterm-uds` and `async_ossl` default to `async-asupersync`, but today they only expose blocking `Read`/`Write` wrappers plus optional `async_io::IoSafe`.
- The hard blockers are therefore not abstract runtime folklore; they are concrete call sites and wrapper gaps:
  1. local Unix / mux-server dispatch path
  2. SSH proxy / pipe path
  3. TLS/OpenSSL path

Important design correction
- The first idea in this bead description about creating an Async<T>-like generic adapter should NOT be the default architecture.
- Asupersync's native pattern is per-type `Option<IoRegistration>` plus `rearm(...)` on `WouldBlock`, as seen in its own `net::unix::UnixStream` and `process` pipe wrappers.
- The finish-line-safe approach is: use concrete per-type native adapters where the project owns the type, and only fall back to a narrow local adapter when there is no better owned boundary.

Recommended implementation slicing
1. Local Unix + mux-server dispatch first.
   files: `frankenterm/uds/src/lib.rs`, `crates/frankenterm-mux-server-impl/src/dispatch.rs`, `frankenterm/client/src/client.rs`, relevant `Cargo.toml` files.
   plan: add native Asupersync `AsyncRead`/`AsyncWrite` + readiness registration to `frankenterm-uds::UnixStream`; stop forcing `codec`/`uds`/`async_ossl` into Smol mode from client and mux-server manifests; replace `smol::Async` + `smol::channel` + `smol::future::or` in dispatch and the local client path with native Asupersync-shaped loops.

2. SSH proxy / pipe path second.
   files: `frankenterm/client/src/client.rs`, possibly `frankenterm/ssh/*` only if needed.
   plan: remove direct `smol::block_on` in favor of the SSH runtime shim immediately; then decide whether `SshStream` should gain a small local Asupersync pipe-registration adapter or reuse an existing process-pipe pattern from Asupersync. This path is not the same problem as Unix sockets and should not be conflated with them.

3. TLS/OpenSSL path third, coordinated with finish-line networking work.
   files: `frankenterm/client/src/client.rs`, `frankenterm/async_ossl/src/lib.rs`.
   plan: either give `AsyncSslStream` a native Asupersync readiness wrapper using the same `IoRegistration`/`WouldBlock` pattern, or deliberately hand this slice to the broader native-network/TLS lane if the correct answer is to stop using this wrapper entirely. Do not hide TLS behind another executor-neutral shim.

Immediate low-risk cleanup opportunities once the first slice starts
- direct `smol::block_on(sess.exec(...))` in `client.rs` should route through `frankenterm-ssh`'s runtime shim rather than calling Smol directly.
- `smol::Timer::after(...)` in `client.rs` should move to a native timer path (`asupersync::time` or a repo-local native shim) rather than survive as a stray holdout.

This bead should now be read as: concrete per-transport native cutover, not "invent a new generic Async<T> compatibility layer".
